case_study_insert.main_stem: Northline Transit & Logistics (NTL) is a private limited company in the road freight and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2011 by Elena Marsh, it delivers palletised goods for regional manufacturers and runs a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. NTL plans to invest $720,000 in a fleet of fuel-efficient trucks and a computerised stock control system, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan and $320,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently handles 32,000 units a year. NTL faces an operational problem: driver absenteeism has reached 8% and late deliveries are rising, while its depot reports growing fuel waste from older vehicles.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Depot Operations and Market Report — Q3 2025: The fleet completed 8,000 consignments last quarter at a late-delivery rate of 4.5%, down from 6.8% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 26 per month. Average delivery time is 2.8 days. Vehicle defect rate rose to 3.2% from 1.9%, and fuel waste is estimated at 7% of mileage. Market research of 500 manufacturers found that 62% would pay up to $0.50 more for guaranteed next-day delivery, and 58% rank reliability above price. A training review shows 18 of 60 drivers have not completed on-the-job training on the new route-planning system; off-the-job training at the regional college is also under consideration.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Northline Transit & Logistics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.8% from $12.60 to $13.33 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across the transport sector. (3) Diesel and vehicle input costs have risen 9.5% year-on-year and road-fuel inflation is 7.2%, while demand for next-day freight grew 4.1%.

questions.question_text: NTL plans to fund part of its $720,000 fleet expansion with $320,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for NTL of using retained profit instead of the $400,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs NTL no interest or capital repayments, which protects cash flow while the business already carries fixed costs of $240,000 a year and is servicing a $400,000 bank loan. Every dollar saved on interest can be spent on tackling the 8% driver absenteeism and the rising late deliveries, for example by supporting the $0.50 next-day delivery promise without raising the $20.00 selling price. With the base rate due to rise to 5.0% (Appendix 3), a variable-rate loan would become more expensive, so retained profit avoids that exposure entirely.

Point 2: Retained profit leaves ownership and control with NTL's existing shareholders and imposes no lender covenants or collateral risk on the $720,000 fleet investment. There is no danger of trucks being repossessed if demand for next-day freight disappoints, which matters because the late-delivery rate is still 4.5% and the depot must first prove the reliability that 62% of surveyed manufacturers want. It also gives NTL quicker, more flexible access to funds than negotiating further debt, letting the automated stock control system be installed before the next peak period.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to NTL and the case data.

questions.question_text: NTL is launching a guaranteed next-day delivery service. Consider national television advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should NTL choose to promote the service? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: A TV campaign would build awareness of next-day delivery very quickly across the whole country and could help NTL win new manufacturing accounts. However, airtime and production are extremely expensive for a 60-employee haulier already funding a $720,000 fleet, and most viewers are outside NTL's regional delivery network, so much of the spend would be wasted.

Local radio sponsorship: Local radio is much cheaper and reaches the regional manufacturers NTL already serves, so it fits the 8,000 consignments a year handled from the depot. Its weakness is limited reach: it cannot build the wider reputation needed when 58% of surveyed customers rank reliability above price and the late-delivery rate is only just down to 4.5%.

Social media influencer marketing: Logistics and business influencers can demonstrate reliable next-day delivery with real tracking data to a targeted audience of e-commerce and manufacturing buyers at low cost per contact. Results build more slowly than television, and credibility depends on the influencer, but the message can directly address the 62% of 500 surveyed manufacturers who would pay $0.50 more for guaranteed next-day delivery.

Recommendation: NTL should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the exact segment identified in the research, costs far less than television, and scales beyond local radio's narrow catchment. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted, and radio is rejected as too limited to support a $400,000 loan-funded expansion; NTL should reinforce the campaign with direct mail to the manufacturers it already supplies.

The campaign can also be measured against the 26 monthly complaints now received, giving NTL a clear baseline for judging whether the new service is genuinely improving reliability rather than simply shifting demand.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to NTL's next-day launch.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some NTL context and emerging judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of NTL's survey data, costs and delivery performance, with a justified recommendation that explains why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: NTL's driver absenteeism has reached 8% and late deliveries are rising. Explain two benefits for NTL of its flat organisational structure and democratic leadership in addressing these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives the 60 drivers a real voice in how routes and shifts are organised, which helps meet their social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Drivers who help set their own schedules are more likely to attend consistently, so NTL can attack the 8% absenteeism rate directly rather than simply replacing drivers, protecting the 8,000 consignments handled each quarter.

Point 2: A flat organisational structure shortens the chain of command, so a late-delivery problem or a 3.2% vehicle defect can be reported and fixed quickly without passing through several management layers. Combined with democratic leadership, this encourages drivers to share practical ideas on route planning and fuel-efficient driving, which can reduce the 7% fuel waste and push the 4.5% late-delivery rate down further, strengthening the reliability that 58% of surveyed manufacturers value most.

Staff involvement also makes the 18 drivers still to complete on-the-job training more receptive to the new route-planning routines, so the $720,000 investment delivers its intended fuel savings instead of being resisted on the depot floor.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to NTL and the case data.

questions.question_text: NTL needs drivers who can use the new route-planning system. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional college. Which should NTL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training at the depot uses NTL's own vehicles and route-planning system, so it is directly relevant and keeps all 18 affected drivers productive while they learn. It protects the 8,000 consignments handled each quarter and avoids losing delivery capacity while the 4.5% late-delivery rate is being improved. However, the trainers are working drivers whose own routes suffer, bad habits can be passed on, and there is no external certificate, which could matter if manufacturers ask for proof of competence.

Off-the-job training: A regional college course gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised qualification for all 18 drivers, which may impress the manufacturers who rank reliability above price. Its drawbacks are the course fees on top of a $720,000 fleet investment, the loss of drivers from the depot during training, and generic content that may not match NTL's exact vehicles, meaning follow-up coaching would still be needed.

Decision: NTL should choose on-the-job training as the main method, with short college sessions later for senior drivers. On-the-job training is cheaper, vehicle-specific and avoids cutting capacity while absenteeism is 8%; full off-the-job training is rejected because the fees and the withdrawal of 18 drivers would disrupt deliveries and threaten the 62% of customers willing to pay $0.50 more for guaranteed next-day delivery.

A blended approach also spreads the risk of 8% absenteeism: if one group is away, other drivers already understand the system. The regional college course can be scheduled in small batches so that only a few drivers are off the road at once, keeping the 4.5% late-delivery rate from worsening while the $400,000 loan is serviced and the 8,000 quarterly consignments are maintained.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little application to NTL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of both methods in NTL's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensively evaluates both methods against cost, disruption and relevance, with a clear decision and explicit reasons for rejecting the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how NTL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($20.00 − $8.00) = $240,000 ÷ $12.00 = 20,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 20,000 consignments a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $20.00 − $8.00 = $12.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways NTL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing break-even output of 20,000 units with actual output of 32,000 units gives a margin of safety of 12,000 units, showing the fleet can absorb a demand dip before making a loss.
2. Contribution per unit of $12.00 lets managers test the $0.50 next-day premium: even a small discount can be modelled against the $240,000 fixed costs before offering it.
3. Knowing that each consignment contributes $12.00 helps judge whether the $400,000 bank loan can be serviced from the 12,000-unit margin of safety before further capital is committed.
4. Average total cost of $15.50 a unit ($240,000 ÷ 32,000 = $7.50, plus $8.00) can be benchmarked each quarter to monitor the 7% fuel waste and the 9.5% rise in diesel input costs.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 20,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $12.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 12,000 units against 32,000-unit output; pricing the $0.50 next-day premium; testing loan affordability on the $720,000 fleet plan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $15.50 to attack 7% fuel waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NTL's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has NTL's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 25.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit $800,000 ÷ revenue $2,000,000 × 100 = 40.0; 2025 $1,125,000 ÷ $2,500,000 × 100 = 45.0. Operating profit $250,000 ÷ revenue $2,000,000 × 100 = 12.5 in 2024 and $375,000 ÷ $2,500,000 × 100 = 15.0 in 2025. Returns on capital: $250,000 ÷ $1,250,000 × 100 = 20.0 in 2024 and $375,000 ÷ $1,500,000 × 100 = 25.0 in 2025. Cost of sales rose from $1,200,000 to $1,375,000, but revenue grew faster, from $2,000,000 to $2,500,000, so gross profit climbed by $325,000. Interest payable fell from $30,000 to $25,000, also helping the operating result.

Evaluation: Every measure moved favourably. The gross margin improved from 40.0% to 45.0%, showing better control of direct freight costs despite dearer diesel. The operating margin rose from 12.5% to 15.0%, so more of each revenue dollar survives fixed costs such as the $240,000 a year. Returns on capital jumped from 20.0% to 25.0%, meaning the $1,500,000 of capital employed is being used far more effectively. These gains are genuine because they are not caused by cutting prices or by a one-off: revenue and gross profit both grew. The main caution is that the late-delivery rate is still 4.5% and absenteeism is 8%, which could raise costs and reverse the trend if the $720,000 fleet is not managed well.

Conclusion: NTL's financial performance has clearly improved. The gross margin (40.0% to 45.0%), operating margin (12.5% to 15.0%) and returns on capital (20.0% to 25.0%) all rose together, and the improvement is supported by higher revenue and gross profit rather than accounting effects. NTL should now protect the gain by using part of the retained profit to cut absenteeism and late deliveries.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or simple changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates all three ratios for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest, and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NTL of replacing older vehicles with fuel-efficient trucks.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Fuel-efficient trucks directly reduce the 7% of mileage currently lost as fuel waste and cushion the 9.5% rise in diesel and vehicle input costs reported in Appendix 3. Lower fuel use cuts the $8.00 variable cost per unit, protecting the $12.00 contribution and making the $720,000 fleet investment easier to justify from the 12,000-unit margin of safety. Cleaner trucks also support the reliability that 58% of surveyed manufacturers rank above price.

Disadvantage: The $720,000 outlay adds to fixed costs and must be funded alongside a $400,000 bank loan while interest rates rise to 5.0%, so cash flow could be tight if next-day demand grows more slowly than the 4.1% forecast. New trucks may also need driver training on the new route-planning system, which is difficult while absenteeism is 8% and the vehicle defect rate has risen to 3.2%; until drivers are confident, the 4.5% late-delivery rate might worsen rather than improve.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to NTL and the case data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.0%, the 5.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in diesel and vehicle input costs will affect NTL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate (4.25% to 5.0%): If NTL's $400,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $400,000 = $3,000 a year (0.0075 × $400,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $240,000 a year, and it would be zero if the loan is fixed-rate. Higher rates may also make consumers warier of premium next-day freight and raise the cost of any future borrowing, but NTL can largely neutralise this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.8%, to $13.33 an hour): With a workforce of 60 in driving and depot roles, this feeds into the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be invented; the honest test is productivity, 32,000 units ÷ 60 staff = about 533 units per worker. If output per worker holds or rises, the extra wages are affordable; if absenteeism of 8% pushes it down, unit labour cost rises and the $12.00 contribution shrinks.

Input-cost inflation (9.5% diesel and vehicles): The $8.00 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound can be calculated: if the whole $8.00 rose 9.5%, that adds 9.5% × $8.00 = $0.76 a unit; across 32,000 units a year that is about $24,320 (32,000 × $0.76). That would cut contribution from $12.00 towards $11.24 on every consignment, and it compounds on top of the existing 7% fuel waste. Only part of it can be recovered through the $0.50 next-day premium.

Conclusion: The 9.5% rise in diesel and vehicle input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 32,000 consignments and erodes the $12.00 contribution that justifies the $720,000 expansion, whereas the interest rise is a bounded $3,000 a year and the wage rise can be absorbed if productivity holds. NTL should cut the 7% fuel waste first.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to NTL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on NTL's costs, revenue or financing in context, using insert figures.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in NTL's context with a well-justified judgement that input cost inflation has the greatest impact and clear reasons why the other two are smaller.
